title: The First Counterattacks
subtitle: Counterattacks, broken communications and the widening northern war
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: Soviet armour delayed German formations in Lithuania and Ukraine, but shortages and broken communications prevented local attacks from becoming a coordinated recovery of the front.
body:
An attack timed to the hour

Poluboyarov’s report of 23 June, sent at 5:50 a.m., records a counterattack being assembled through personal intervention in a failing communications system. After visiting commanders, he assigned starts at eleven and noon so that two mechanised corps could converge in time. The army meant to coordinate them, however, had contact with neither front headquarters nor the corps. His requests for aircraft, fuel and ammunition identified what the projected counterattack still lacked, even after its commanders had received their objectives and starting times. By 25 June, that distance had become central to the Soviet effort to recover the initiative in Lithuania and western Ukraine. [1] The same problem confronted Soviet resistance across much of the invaded frontier. The Red Army was counterattacking, sometimes with determination and considerable local force. It was not standing aside while German columns passed. But attacking formations had to find the enemy, reach their assembly areas and cooperate with neighbours whose whereabouts were uncertain. German commanders could therefore encounter a dangerous tank attack on one road while another formation continued advancing beyond it. The Soviet difficulties were organisational and physical as well as tactical: a tank that could defeat an opposing vehicle could still become useless for want of fuel, a passable crossing or an order that reached its crew in time. [2] The fighting around Raseiniai illustrates that distinction particularly well. Here the Soviet command tried to strike the flank of Army Group North’s advance and protect the retreat of its rifle formations. The attack imposed a real battle on German armoured troops, but it did not restore the front. In western Ukraine, a larger concentration of Soviet mechanised corps was still developing its own counterstroke. Meanwhile, the war was becoming open and unmistakable in Finland, and German conquest in Lithuania was already bringing organised anti-Jewish violence. These were connected developments, although they cannot be reduced to a single narrative of tanks racing east. [3] The dated map provides a framework for comparing these uneven operations. Its German reference sheet records an evening assessment, including penetrations and reported opposing formations. It should be read with the Soviet orders and reports, which disclose intended movements, missing information and attempts to sustain forces still fighting behind the leading German positions. The sources answer different questions: the sheet locates the main operational dangers as perceived by German headquarters, while the Soviet records help explain why the attempted response developed as it did. Their comparison supports a regional interpretation, without establishing possession of every locality between the depicted lines. [4]

The roads through Lithuania

Field Marshal Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb’s Army Group North had three principal instruments. Georg von Küchler’s 18th Army advanced on the Baltic side; Ernst Busch’s 16th Army operated farther inland; Erich Hoepner’s Fourth Panzer Group supplied the mobile striking force between and ahead of them. Its two motorised corps followed different routes. Georg-Hans Reinhardt’s XLI Corps encountered the Soviet armour around Raseiniai and the Dubysa, while Erich von Manstein’s LVI Corps drove farther east towards the Western Dvina crossing at Daugavpils, also called Dvinsk. Their common purpose was to break the Soviet armies in the Baltic region and open the approach towards Leningrad. Their immediate experiences were already diverging. [5] The rivers explain much of the operational geometry. The Niemen lay near the opening battlefield; the Dubysa divided routes through central Lithuania; the Western Dvina offered a much larger defensive barrier farther northeast. German success depended on crossing these obstacles before Soviet forces could organise behind them. Soviet success required more than the survival of a bridgehead or a single division. It required withdrawing troops to reach a new line, headquarters to establish communications and reserves to arrive before the attackers converted a crossing into a route for their whole formation. Roads and bridges made that a race with a limited number of possible destinations. [5] Fyodor Kuznetsov commanded the Soviet Northwestern Front. Pyotr Sobennikov’s 8th Army covered the northwestern part of the threatened area, with Vasily Morozov’s 11th Army farther south. Their deployment had already been disrupted by the initial German blows. Kuznetsov’s directive of 22 June identified the German penetration towards Tauragė as a threat to the 8th Army and ordered the Third and 12th Mechanised Corps to intervene. The Twelfth was to turn against the flank and rear of the advancing Germans. The Third was to bring its Second Tank and Eighty-fourth Motorised Divisions towards Raseiniai, while leaving its 5th Tank Division with the 11th Army. That qualification matters: the 3rd Corps was not entering this battle with all the formations listed under its name in a prewar inventory. [6] The order also assigned Sobennikov responsibility for coordinating the two corps and directed the air force to strike German concentrations. This was a combined operation in conception, with armour, aviation, antitank defence and the retreating infantry intended to support one another. Its weakness lay in the widening distance between that conception and the actual condition of the command system. The same directive was trying to prevent encirclement, arrange a counterattack and prepare positions east of the Niemen. Headquarters was already pursuing several urgent tasks with forces whose freedom of movement was shrinking. [6]

Raseiniai and the broken counterstroke

Poluboyarov’s report gives the counterstroke a more precise shape than the broad arrows usually drawn over Lithuania. Alexey Kurkin’s 3rd Mechanised Corps was to move west from Raseiniai towards the Tauragė–Šiauliai road, then turn southwest towards Tauragė and Tilsit. Nikolai Shestopalov’s 12th Corps was to advance southwest on the other side of that road. The intention was to bring converging pressure against the German penetration rather than simply send tanks forward wherever fighting could be heard. Poluboyarov had even arranged a coded coordination table. His chosen attack times, eleven and noon on 23 June, provide a contemporary benchmark against which the operation can be judged. [1] Poluboyarov’s timetable supplies a contemporary measure of intent, but the report does not show the two corps attacking at the required strength and time. It explicitly identifies the communications failure that made coordination precarious. Personal visits and a coded table were efforts to compensate for that failure, rather than evidence that commanders had ignored the problem. The requested air cover and supplies still had to be delivered while German forces continued moving. This is the operational significance of the document: a precisely expressed plan could remain dependent on arrangements that had not yet become functioning capabilities. [1] Around Raseiniai, Soviet heavy tanks made that incomplete attack tactically formidable. The German 6th Panzer Division encountered vehicles against which some of its customary antitank weapons were inadequate. German battle groups had to combine heavier guns, manoeuvre and close action instead of assuming that their normal armament would settle every encounter. The best-known episode involved a KV tank blocking the Raseiniai–Šiluva road and interrupting contact between two German battle groups. Archival research by Alvydas Žardinskas places this incident within the division’s actual communications problem, correcting retellings that inflate it into the immobilisation of an entire invading army. [7]

A famous encounter

One tank and the scale of a claim

A roadblock could be important without stopping Army Group North. The Raseiniai KV interrupted a particular German division’s communications and required repeated efforts to destroy it. That is a substantial tactical achievement. Expanding it into a halt imposed on every German formation removes the geography that makes the incident intelligible. [7]

The Soviet evening summary for 24 June is more revealing about the wider battle than any isolated duel. It claimed a major success for the 2nd Tank Division, including large German equipment losses, but also reported that the division was around Raseiniai without fuel. German reserves had arrived and were attacking. The front was considering delivering fuel by aircraft. The same report said that the effect of the 12th Mechanised Corps’ operations could not be felt and blamed Shestopalov’s inactivity. These are statements by an embattled headquarters, not findings from an impartial inquiry. The German losses cannot simply be accepted as audited totals, and the accusation against the commander must be read beside the earlier admission that communications were broken. [2] The records therefore support a conclusion about the failure of sustained coordination while preserving evidence of formidable local resistance. Soviet tanks could disrupt German movement, but the formations employing them were losing the capacity to replenish, communicate and act together. That deterioration reduced the duration and reach of their tactical effects. German commanders could contain an obstacle on one route while exploiting movement on another, so the Soviet effort did not restore the coherence of the front. The distinction explains why German accounts of difficult encounters and Soviet evidence of operational defeat need not contradict each other. [2] [4]

A retreat that could not move as one

The Northwestern Front’s reports show that the tank battle was only one part of a larger disintegration. On the Baltic coast, the Sixty-seventh Rifle Division was fighting around Liepāja, called Libau in German records. The front reported heavy fighting, bombing of the harbour, airfield and railway station, fires in the city and the loss of communications. Farther inland, units of the 11th Army had lost much of their equipment and were attempting to reorganise around Babtai, Jonava and Vepriai. The whereabouts of the 128th Rifle Division were unknown to front headquarters. Each of these statements describes a different condition; none can be represented adequately by saying that the Northwestern Front had simply vanished. [2] The report also followed a German motorised column moving towards Šiauliai after a breakthrough between Kražiai and Kelmė during the previous evening. That direction threatened the connections behind the Soviet troops fighting around Raseiniai. Elsewhere in the same army, part of the 11th Rifle Division was organising a new defensive line while the rest had yet to arrive from Narva. The problem was therefore not only replacing losses suffered in battle. A commander might be expected to defend a position with a formation whose remaining components were still approaching from far away, while an enemy column was already turning the roads behind it into a battlefield. [2] Retreat brought together formations in markedly different conditions. Some retained positions and communications, others were travelling or assembling, and some could no longer be located by front headquarters. Their movements consequently could not be synchronised through a complete common picture. A road held open by one unit might lose its value when a neighbouring route was cut, while an otherwise reasonable order could arrive after the circumstances that justified it had changed. The reports’ references to positions still unconfirmed are therefore substantive military evidence. They indicate the uncertainty through which command had to operate, rather than merely gaps for a later map to conceal. [2] The consequences became unmistakable immediately after the date of this study. At ten in the evening on 26 June, Kuznetsov ordered an effort to rescue the 2nd Tank Division, now described as encircled and without fuel. A strong tank battalion was to carry fuel and shells, approach unexpectedly through the German rear towards Raseiniai and enable the division to escape towards Šiauliai. The action was ordered for the following morning. This is evidence of the intended rescue, not proof that the necessary battalion reached the stranded formation or that the division emerged intact. It nevertheless shows how quickly the purpose of Soviet armour had changed: from cutting into the German advance to opening a passage for its own survival. [8] That later order must not be moved backwards onto the 25 June map. Nor should the German seizure of the Daugavpils bridges on 26 June be treated as an achievement already completed the previous evening. The point of keeping these dates separate is practical. While Reinhardt’s corps fought through the Raseiniai area, Manstein’s route offered a different opportunity towards the Dvina. The German mobile advance was composed of several moving parts. Soviet resistance against one of them did not automatically protect the crossings threatened by another. [5]

The larger armoured battle forming in Ukraine

Farther south, the counterattack problem appeared on a greater scale. Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South was advancing with Ewald von Kleist’s First Panzer Group, supported by Walter von Reichenau’s 6th Army on the northern part of the sector and Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army farther south. Mikhail Kirponos’s Southwestern Front possessed substantial mechanised forces, but their locations, movements and changing assignments prevented them from becoming a single concentrated weapon at the moment of the German crossing. The geography of Lutsk, Dubno, Brody and the approaches from Lwów created opportunities to strike the German penetration from different directions. It also created long and congested routes along which those forces first had to arrive. [9] Kirponos’s order issued at Tarnopol at nine on the evening of 24 June specified an attack at seven the following morning. The Eighth, Fifteenth and 4th Mechanised Corps were named in the intended operation, which was to defeat the German mobile grouping north of the Shchurovytse–Dmytriv–Mosty Velyki line and reach the Voynytsia–Mylatyn–Sokal area. One purpose was to avert the encirclement of Mikhail Potapov’s 5th Army. The order required units to occupy their starting positions during the night and commanders to verify that subordinates understood their tasks. These were concrete instructions with a date and an hour, not a vague exhortation to counterattack. [10] The aviation arrangements were equally exact on paper. Reconnaissance was to identify targets before 6.50; the strongest opening air strike was to take place in the ten minutes before seven; successive attacks were to support the armour afterwards. Tanks would mark themselves with red rockets and folded white sheets, and aircraft would signal recognition by rocking a wing. Such details reveal both a serious effort at cooperation and the fragility of the methods available. A timetable this precise depended on formations arriving together, pilots finding the intended targets and tank units distinguishing friendly aircraft while already under pressure. [10] By late on 25 June, a new order prescribed another attack for the next morning. The Eighth and 15th Mechanised Corps were again central, now joined in the wider design by the Ninth and Nineteenth under Potapov’s control southwest of Lutsk. Assembly was required by 4.30 and the attack by nine on 26 June. The target was the German grouping around Radekhiv, and the northern corps were to assist by attacking along the Lutsk–Brody railway. This revised programme is direct evidence that the intended result of the previous order had not been secured on its stated terms. It does not establish that nothing had happened on 25 June; it establishes that the desired coordinated defeat of the German force remained ahead rather than behind. [11]

Cooperation prescribed in detail

Sheets, rockets and a missing map

Southwestern Front order 0015 of 24 June prescribed red rockets and folded white sheets to identify tanks to supporting aircraft, with aircraft signalling by rocking a wing. The published collection also notes that the map repeatedly cited in the order was not found in the archive. The text therefore preserves recognition procedures and named objectives more securely than the complete graphic arrangement. It establishes intended cooperation, while the arrival and effect of supporting sorties require separate evidence.

[10]
The full consequences of these battles belong to the study for 1 July. On the 25th, the important comparison with Lithuania is already clear. Both fronts were trying to strike German mobile forces on their flanks. Both depended on corps whose arrival and communications were uncertain. Ukraine offered a larger and more sustained armoured response, but a greater number of tanks did not abolish the problems of timing, fuel and command. Its battles would develop over several days, and their outcome should not be imposed prematurely on the men receiving orders that evening.

Finland’s passage into open war

The northern war acquired another public turning point on 25 June when Soviet aircraft attacked targets in Finland. The American minister in Helsinki, H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, reported a conversation that evening with Foreign Minister Rolf Witting. Witting said that Finland was again at war and that the government would make its position clear to the Diet. He also emphasised that Finland was no longer alone and referred to German assistance. The dispatch captures the Finnish government’s immediate presentation of the event, rather than a later reconstruction written after the outcome was known. [12] The air attacks were a real escalation, but they did not create German–Finnish military cooperation out of nothing. German troops were already deployed in Finland, and preparations for operations against the Soviet Union had been coordinated before Barbarossa began. The Finnish leadership sought to recover territory lost in the Winter War and pursued its own national objectives, while the German command sought strategic benefits against the Soviet north. Those aims overlapped sufficiently to produce military cooperation without making Finland’s war identical in every respect to Germany’s. The distinction helps explain Finnish decision-making; it does not make the prior preparations disappear. [5] Finland’s transition to open war has to be reconstructed through the separate dates of cooperation, deployment, attack and political declaration. German forces and prior military arrangements already connected Finland to the eastern campaign before the Soviet air attacks of 25 June. Those attacks then enabled the government to present the conflict publicly as a renewed defensive struggle. Schoenfeld’s report records both that presentation and Witting’s recognition of the strategic difference made by German support. The combination explains the government’s immediate position more precisely than either a picture of untouched neutrality or an assumption that every Finnish operation began on Germany’s timetable. [12] For the wider campaign, the immediate significance was the enlargement of the Soviet command’s obligations. Forces and attention had to be assigned across a northern theatre reaching far beyond the Baltic advance. Yet it would be equally inaccurate to paint that entire theatre as a single moving front on 25 June. The German reference sheet extends into Finland precisely because the military problem was geographically broad. Its inclusion of deployments should not be confused with proof that every planned offensive was already under way. [4]

Conquest and murder in Kaunas

While Soviet units struggled to withdraw through Lithuania, Jews in Kaunas faced a danger for which the operational maps provide almost no adequate language. In his subsequent report covering the period to 15 October, Einsatzgruppe A commander Walter Stahlecker described efforts to encourage local anti-Jewish violence while concealing German direction. His account identified the night of 25–26 June as a major pogrom and credited a Lithuanian group led by Klimaitis with carrying it out after prompting from a German advance detachment. The report’s vocabulary attempted to turn murder into an administrative achievement. Its explicit concern with making German involvement invisible is particularly important evidence. [13] Stahlecker’s report must be read as a perpetrator’s account addressed to superiors. Its totals and presentation of organisational effectiveness cannot be accepted as a neutral census, but its discussion of instigation and concealment provides direct evidence about policy. It describes the use of local participants while managing the appearance of German responsibility. That evidence identifies the agency of the security organisation and of the perpetrators it encouraged; it does not assign collective responsibility to an entire national population. Source criticism here sharpens the account of culpability by distinguishing what the document discloses from the claims through which its author sought to commend his work. [13] The setting was a society recently subjected to Soviet occupation and repression. German propaganda and local antisemites converted anger at Soviet rule into accusations against Jews as a collective. That accusation was false, and it supplied no defence for murder. The prisoners, families and neighbourhoods attacked were not interchangeable with the Soviet government. Keeping this distinction explicit is necessary because the perpetrators themselves tried to blur it. Their claim to be eliminating a political enemy was part of the machinery of persecution. [13]

Evidence of concealment

A report that describes its own deception

Stahlecker wanted anti-Jewish attacks to appear locally initiated without visible German orders. A photograph of local perpetrators would therefore not, by itself, disprove German instigation. The report makes the management of appearances part of the evidence historians must examine. [13]

The timing places this violence within the opening advance. Capture of crossings and towns enabled security detachments to move, obtain local assistance and attack Jewish inhabitants while military operations continued. The connection should be explained without collapsing distinct experiences into one: soldiers’ supply failures and civilians’ exposure to organised murder had different immediate causes and perpetrators. Their histories intersected through the conquest that changed who could exercise force in a locality. Following only the foremost armoured formations would omit that transformation in power, even though it was already shaping the consequences of German progress.

What the counterattacks changed

By the evening of 25 June, the Soviet counterattacks had demonstrated that German tactical superiority did not mean immunity from resistance. Armour could be checked, communications interrupted and individual German formations forced to fight hard for routes that a campaign map reduced to a line. The same evidence shows why such achievements did not amount to a strategic reversal. The Soviet attacks had not restored dependable communications, reopened the whole frontier or prevented German formations on other axes from advancing. The Northwestern Front’s own reports, with their mixture of local success claims, missing units and requests for fuel, are the clearest record of that contradiction. [2] There is no need to invent a German deadline for every town to measure this result. The documented Soviet attack hours and objectives provide a sufficient standard: the intended coordinated blows had not produced their assigned operational effect. On the German side, the larger objective of destroying Soviet forces before they could consolidate farther east remained in progress. Continued Soviet resistance complicated that task, but the armoured penetrations were still threatening the routes through which a coherent retreat would have to pass. [1] [11] [5] The counterattacks had imposed costs and interruptions without restoring the communications and freedom of movement needed for a coherent Soviet defence. In the central sector, those conditions were deteriorating on a still larger scale as German mobile forces approached Minsk and Soviet armies farther west sought routes out. The [next study](/articles/barbarossa-the-encirclement-of-minsk-1941-06-28) follows that transition from threatened withdrawal to encirclement. There, formations continued fighting even as the headquarters, communications and supply arrangements needed to sustain a common defence were breaking apart.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Soviet operational records are cited from the General Staff’s published documentary collections, accessed in transcription; archival identifiers are those printed in those collections. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
